I came close to thinking that way a couple years ago, but I've become more optimistic. There is no shortage of problems that can be solved (in fact, wants are infinite), and LLMs may actually enable our profession to reliably deliver them better than 50% completion.

I've also seen non-technical folks in the corporate and government worlds glom onto vibe coding, only to start flailing like they were caught in a rip current when the underlying technical debt is too strong, even with strong and capable models.

For a certain type of engineer who enjoys really arcane technical problems, yeah, the gravy train may be over, or at least will involve a lot more machines than it used to, as Alan Turing predicted about "mechanical work" becoming a "drudge."[0]

And I think Big Tech is for the foreseeable future a sink for capital in the form of specialized hardware rather than human capital.

The arcane technical problems aspect of the job has always been changing; LLMs are just a continuation of the trend.

I'm old enough to remember when compiled languages like C were bemoaned by people because their skill at crafting assembly by hand was suddenly less important. Or similarly with people who were brilliant with arithmetic, or symbolic manipulation, or manual drafting/lettering. These skills were all paramount at one time, and it's natural that the people who excelled at them will feel a sense of loss.

The real goal, however, will always be to solve real-world problems. Engineering consists of whatever gets you there most effectively.

children.author: tkamat29
children.textRawHtml:
Why would you want to hone in on finding "good programmers" though? Programming is not the end-all be-all skill of being a good software engineer, this was true even before AI but is even more true now.

Leetcode is popular because:

1. It gauges problem solving ability and pattern recognition, which are essential to any job, and particularly useful for software engineers.

2. It is language agnostic - most jobs would rather have a strong engineer that doesn't know their particular language/tech stack than a weak engineer that is familiar with the stack.

3. It has objective evaluation criteria (correctness + time/space complexity).

It's certainly not perfect, but I have yet to see an alternative that accomplishes all of the above. The one thing I can see potentially complementing it is the new style of AI-assisted assessment where you are dropped into an unknown codebase, and asked to make fixes/features that are assisted by an AI agent. This solves the language-agnostic issue with pre-AI versions of these interviews, where you had to have memorized specific tech stack features or language syntax in order to accomplish the task. Now AI can take care of that stuff, and the interviewee can focus on the problem solving aspect.

children.author: timr
children.textRawHtml:
> It gauges problem solving ability and pattern recognition, which are essential to any job, and particularly useful for software engineers.

Proof of claim required. Leetcode primarily measure's someone's ability to memorize leetcode problems, and secondarily measures their ability to vomit this knowledge up in a stressful situation.

There's an entire test-prep industry surrounding this interview method. Any undergrad will tell you that the way you pass leetcode interviews is to "grind". You'd have to be oblivious to not realize that the system has been gamed to hell and back.

Since you are just asserting things, I will assert a simpler explanation: the primary reason Leetcode is popular is because it is cheap. If you have the problem that you have too many applicants and don't want to spend money interviewing them all, you have to come up with an efficient filter that doesn't violate hiring laws. You don't particularly care if the false negative rate is high, so a test of superficially relevant trivia is what you do. Even better if the trivia can be validated by computer!

Setting aside the fact that almost no companies actually had this problem outside of FAANG, thanks to AI, the approach has gone from "somewhat relevant" to "completely irrelevant" within a couple of years. It's time to take it out back and shoot it.

I think this (and MITs precedent) makes an important claim about the value of higher ed: the value of an undergraduate education is not just access to curriculum, certification, or the admissions filter. Openness is an act of confidence that all the rest matters, too: the quality of instruction (and that is more than just lectures and distributed materials), the structure and guidance, the spirit of comity, immersion in academic values, having one's beliefs challenged, engaging in diverse ways of thinking.

For all of their flaws, I think universities are one of our greatest inventions and it's a mistake to view them purely in economic/transactional terms.

Yes [0]. For a single node you can just use this, it works like the Golang/language rate limiters you might already be familiar with [1]

In a multiple node/distributed architecture you need away to coordinate rate limits across nodes and not try to fight the CAP theorem.

children.author: gerdesj
children.textRawHtml:
Quite. The public DNS is absolutely the wrong way to go about this. However there is nothing wrong with fiddling with DNS "internally" - that's a different issue.

It's all about truth and messaging.

DNS tells you where something is, no more and no less. When queried, it points to the map and says: "It's there, off you trot". DNS does not care what is there, it is just a guide.

DNS works over port 53/udp+tcp and could be fiddled with in transit. There is a variety of DNS called DNSSEC which, with care, can be trusted to be accurate (for your given value of accurate).

Messaging: As I said, port 53/udp+tcp could be fiddled with if DNSSEC is not in play. There is also DNS over HTTPS or DoH. Now the messaging channel is encrypted. At this point you have the same confidence in security as you do when looking at https web sites.

Now, you can obviously use DoH DNS from anywhere in the world and it will look like ordinary web traffic. Most browsers are already doing this.

Messing with DNS now in Europe is basically fiddling whilst Rome burns - bloody stupid and couterproductive. Hamstringing a service such as Quad9 is at best ridiculous.

> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. > There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.

I think anthropic is now buying books and then scanning them. It's an aspect of doctrine of first sale that publishers really don't like. Don't forget that the Lion's share of the first sale money goes to the publisher.

And this is yet another example of where credit for a work needs to be separate from copyright and just like copyright gives you standing to sue to enforce your right to seek rent, credit should give you standing to sue if somebody doesn't give you the credit for the work. Of course, this means that simultaneous or parallel development of a work should be part of the acknowledgement.

Although giving credit could be interesting. For example, if you develop a picture of a black cat, do you have to give credit to every person that's ever developed a picture of a black cat in all media and forms?

children.author: tonic_note
children.textRawHtml:
Yeah, this is the thing that I think everyone misses when they talk about how notifications on iOS are fucked. They're always quibbling over the grouping, the presentation, and the organization, but what actually needs to happen is the user needs to be given full granular control over every single type of notification that an app can send. Apps should be required to catalog every single notification, and I should be able to choose which ones I want.

There are tons of useful notifications I would like to get, but I end up having to choose the nuclear option of turning them off completely because I know that by allowing notifications, I expose myself to vomit-inducing growth hack spam.

Android has per-app notification channels that let you mute notifications by category for each app.

Sadly, the biggest Android OEM (Samsung) has decided to hide this feature in the settings app, meaning lots of users don't even know about it.

It also requires app developers to categorise their push notifications themselves, which they often refuse to do, despite Play Store guidelines requiring it.
